1.pericope_label: Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment. Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow. He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the argument the court exists to settle, claiming the conqueror's rise as the work of the God exalted above idols and proving it by what that career does, destruction for the idolatrous nations and release for God's people, while noting the condition it rests on, that the conqueror must already be under way since an unfulfilled event proves nothing; they name Cyrus, and read the march as unhindered along a route never walked before; Ellicott hears irony in the call to renew strength, pictures the prophet seeing the far future open, renders the clause as the man whom Righteousness calls to tread in his steps, insists on the coming restorer and mentions the patriarchal reading only to reject it, prefers a present tense throughout, and recalls how Assyrian kings boast of leading armies where none had gone.

Gill takes the man for Abraham and marshals the fit, called out of an idolatrous family beyond the river, obedient at once, given a land held by nations, made father of many nations and victor over kings, reporting the Jewish authorities behind that reading; Calvin chooses Abraham for a pastoral reason, that exiles who found return incredible are pointed to an ancestor brought out of the same country through worse dangers by a power not since diminished, turns the challenge inward against a people who had God near them in the law, excuses them by the two diseases of human nature that throw off restraint in prosperity and lie down insensible in adversity, and makes the unknown country evidence of help, since pursuing an enemy through strange ground is the hardest thing in war.

Clarke agrees that the character of righteousness suits the patriarch better and that the alarm of the idol-makers follows naturally on his posterity entering a land they were sent to clear, and stops on a missing preposition that the old versions and one manuscript appear to have read; Wesley names Cyrus, notes that Persia lies due east of Judea and Babylon alike, and observes that the prophet speaks of what is future as though past.

Henry has the summons going out to the remotest islands, distant but not outside the jurisdiction of one who owns the ends of the earth, silence proclaimed while the cause is heard, and advises onlookers watching the two kingdoms contend to keep quiet and expect the verdict rather than object to the proceedings.

debates.question: Who is the righteous man raised up from the east?

positions.position: Abraham, whose character and history fit the description, and whose posterity alarmed the idolaters.
Abraham, chosen for the comfort of exiles who are pointed to an ancestor brought from the same country through worse dangers.
Cyrus, the coming restorer, whom Righteousness calls to tread in his steps.
Cyrus, raised from Persia, which lies east of both Judea and Babylon.

outliers.claim: Points out that the argument only works if the conqueror is already under way, since an event still unfulfilled would carry no force as present proof.
Excuses the people's failure to take comfort by the two complementary diseases of human nature, throwing off restraint in prosperity and lying down insensible in adversity.

themes: Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment.

Who raised up the righteous man from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow.
He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet.

4.pericope_label: Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the Lord, the first, and with the last; I am he. The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came. They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch separate the two verbs as bringing about and carrying out, so that the author is claimed for both the origin and the progress of the event, and take the trembling of the islands as the effect the conqueror's course had already begun to produce, noting that the Hebrew pairs seeing and fearing by sound; Ellicott hears in the closing words the central thought of the nation's creed and the declaration of eternal being that recurs through these chapters, presses what the fear produced, a rush to the shrines with new statues commissioned and idol-making given fresh impetus, and corrects the trade from carpenter to caster, tracing plates laid on the anvil, hammer-smoothing and approved soldering before the last irony of a guardian god nailed down so it will not fall.

Gill says the scheme was contrived and then effected, declines the conquest reading of the trembling islands and applies the verse to the spread of the Gospel with temples abandoned and a panic among priests whose living depended on the old religion, and has the wooden figure finished and the goldsmith hurried into plating it; Calvin widens the appeal deliberately, since the question is not about a single act but a succession of ages, fixes on the ingratitude of a world that shuddered and went straight back to what it was, makes the mutual encouragement worse than the fear and generalises that superstition always begins in men agreeing to darken a light that came from above, and works the disputed craft words out for himself.

Clarke notes that a word has dropped from the text, supplied by an old manuscript and all the versions, and records a conjunction added by three manuscripts that restores the second member to its poetical form, and another added by five manuscripts and the ancient versions; Wesley makes the calling a summoning out of nothing and has the finished image fastened to a wall or pillar.

debates.question: What did the islands see that made them afraid?

positions.position: The victorious course of the conqueror, already begun.
The spread of the Gospel, with idols neglected and temples abandoned.
The mighty work of deliverance, feared lest they be caught in the same calamity.

outliers.claim: Traces the fear to a rush for the shrines rather than to any recognition of the Eternal, with new statues commissioned and idols probably made to be carried into battle.
Generalises from the craftsmen encouraging one another that superstition always begins in men agreeing by mutual consent to darken a light brought to them from heaven.

themes: Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the Lord, the first, and with the last; I am he.
The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came.
They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage.

So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.

8.pericope_label: But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend. Thou whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called thee from the chief men thereof, and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away. Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks this as the first appearance of the servant of the Lord and sets out the idea in three concentric circles, the nation as it stands, the nation realising its ideal, and a single person gathering the ideal into himself, lining them up with an apostle's distinction between the seed after the flesh, the heirs of the patriarch's faith and the one seed who is Christ; he identifies the ends of the earth with the city on the Euphrates at the edge of the prophet's horizon, corrects the chief men to the far-off regions, makes the prophet the herald of election while balancing it against the charge to make one's calling sure, and finds in the verb for strengthening a second sense of attaching to oneself; Keil and Delitzsch turn the exclamation forward to an intervention close at hand in which the men of the quarrel are sought and not found.

Gill reads the servant as the spiritual Israel rather than the natural, men turned from idols to the living God, denies that the ends of the earth means the patriarch or his natural seed, and distinguishes three ways of being present, by essence, by providence and by special grace, insisting on the third; Calvin takes the election as a restraint, since a calling of free grace is no licence to run past bounds and nothing is more absurd than walking like blind men once the sun has risen, notes the movement from one man to a whole people, reads the relative clause as giving past kindness for a reason, and refuses to claim that the promise leaves believers with no fear at all, only that tempted men resist steadily enough to win.

Clarke shows that the disputed word means an arm or extremity and answers in parallel to the ends of the earth in the previous line, and records a conjunction added by many manuscripts which completes the sense; Wesley keeps the traditional rendering of a man called out from among the great persons he lived among, and has the nation brought from a remote country in the loins of its father.

Henry observes that the words are addressed to the nation as to a single person so that any individual may take them to himself, notes how often the caution against fear is repeated, and concludes that it is against the mind of God that his people should be a timorous people.

debates.question: What does the phrase rendered from the chief men mean?

positions.position: From the far-off regions, not the chief men.
From among the great persons the patriarch lived among in Chaldea.
Either that the people were brought from a remote country, or that a God whose dominion reaches the world's edges stretched out his hand to one people only.

outliers.claim: Sets the servant of the Lord in three concentric circles, the nation as it stands, the nation realising its ideal, and a single person who gathers that ideal into himself.
Denies that the promise makes believers wholly free of fear, holding only that distressed and tempted men resist with enough steadiness to secure the victory.

themes: But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend.
Thou whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called thee from the chief men thereof, and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away.
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.

11.pericope_label: Behold, all they that were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confounded: they shall be as nothing; and they that strive with thee shall perish. Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, even them that contended with thee: they that war against thee shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought. For I the Lord thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee. Fear not, thou worm Jacob, and ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the Lord, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff. Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the Lord, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel. When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue faileth for thirst, I the Lord will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together: That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the Lord hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note that the encouragement is repeated to promise not survival only but the upper hand; Ellicott takes the worm as a reminder of having no strength at all in a nation chosen when it was fewest of peoples, notices the shift from masculine to feminine and back when strength given from outside is named, identifies the threshing instrument as a revolving sledge with two-edged blades still used in Syria, lets the promise of water start from the help given returning exiles before it rises into poetry where earthly things are parables of heavenly, admires the varied iteration by which every contour is given the water that suits it, sees a paradise of stately groves and wonders whether four trees and three making seven is deliberate, and says the gifts are meant to make men acknowledge the giver.

Gill hears a league entered and a walk hand in hand, compares a child held by a parent and so afraid of nothing, reports the rabbinic observation about the worm's soft mouth boring the hardest cedar, describes corn crushed under a spiked cart or a weighted drag, recalls threshing floors set on hilltops to catch the wind, applies the thirst to believers lacking nothing in Christ and much in themselves, and has nature's course changed rather than the people want; Calvin explains why the enemies are named at all, distinguishes those who attack by violence from those who attack by slander and lawsuits, defends the apparent insult of the worm since high titles would be absurd in deep wretchedness, presses the reversal by which a people nearly ground to powder is given strength to grind, distinguishes the bruising that does the faithful good from the winnowing that scatters the obstinate, and draws the lesson that God keeps secret methods in reserve.

Clarke draws the application that this people's strength is prayer, by which they cut down the mighty, calls the instrument a corn-drag and passes on the reading that makes the mountains the princes of the nations, reads the planting as shade for travellers fainting in a hot land, and argues that a word for heart has dropped out since every ancient version translates as though it stood there; Wesley states the reversal by which mischief falls on its contrivers, makes the mountains the lofty potentates, notes that mountains bear no rivers, and admits the tree names cannot now be identified.

debates.question: What is promised by the water in the wilderness?

positions.position: A spiritual want and supply, since believers lack nothing in Christ and much in themselves.
A promise starting from the help given returning exiles but rising into poetry where earthly things are parables of heavenly, needing no literal fulfilment.
A real preparation for extreme poverty in exile, thirst being named because nothing distresses men more.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes two kinds of bruising, the faithful broken for their good because they submit to authority, and the obstinate simply blown away like chaff.
Passes on the rabbinic application of the worm, that the strength of this people lies in prayer, by which they cut down the mighty as a soft mouth bores the hardest cedar.

themes: Behold, all they that were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confounded: they shall be as nothing; and they that strive with thee shall perish.
Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, even them that contended with thee: they that war against thee shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought.

21.pericope_label: Produce your cause, saith the Lord; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come. Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and behold it together. Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you. I have raised up one from the north, and he shall come: from the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name: and he shall come upon princes as upon morter, and as the potter treadeth clay. Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, He is righteous? yea, there is none that sheweth, yea, there is none that declareth, yea, there is none that heareth your words. The first shall say to Zion, Behold, behold them: and I will give to Jerusalem one that bringeth good tidings. For I beheld, and there was no man; even among them, and there was no counsellor, that, when I asked of them, could answer a word. Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion.

schools.summary: Ellicott sees the opening scene repeated with worshippers hurrying between oracles, cites the Greek historian on kings and cities consulting shrines about the new conqueror, argues that the former things are the head of what is coming rather than the remote past, compares the taunt on Carmel and asks whether any deity can claim a fortune it announced beforehand, calls the verdict a summing up in the Judge's name, divides the compass between Media and Persia for one conqueror, explains the word for princes as a borrowed title for a satrap, and gives two renderings of the herald while thinking him a messenger reporting victories; Keil and Delitzsch note that the floor was given to the idols and nothing said, and that the argument answers its two earlier charges in turn, ruler and then omniscient.

Gill grants that the material of an idol is gold or brass and denies only its divinity, reporting a rendering of less than nothing, and preserves the alternative that two men are meant rather than one; Calvin adds that exiles hear their hope mocked as credulity so the challenge arms them with God as advocate, heads off the misreading of evil as injustice rather than adversity, distinguishes the denied quality from the undenied substance since nobody adores metal as metal, takes the north for the Babylonians and the east for the Medes and Persians as two revolutions worth remembering, hears a taunt in the offer to acknowledge whoever can do the like, notes that the word rendered righteous can mean approved, and insists prophecy exists to build up the church rather than to inform.

Clarke prefers a rendering calling the images forward as the mighty powers their owners think them, argues from the versions that a letter is corrupted while noting the rabbis deny it, reports two further identifications of the figure from the north, one the Messiah and one the patriarch on the ground that the tenses are past, and paraphrases a transposed sentence into a single announcement; Wesley reads the former things as things shortly to come, turns the second demand into a dare to protect their own and destroy his, explains the northern direction by a Median mother, contingent and colleague, and closes on the words for wind and confusion, the second being the term for the rude heap before creation.

Henry has the idols summoned to make their best case and observes that nothing exposes an absurdity so well as letting its defenders state their reasons, adding that a god must show understanding and active power, both in perfection.

debates.question: Who is the one raised up from the north?

positions.position: Cyrus, north for Media and east for Persia, both under one conqueror.
Two powers, the Babylonians from the north and the Medes and Persians from the east.
Cyrus, though the alternative that two men are meant is preserved.
Others make the figure the Messiah, or apply the whole chapter to the patriarch because the tenses are past.

outliers.claim: Explains the word for evil as adversity sent by providence rather than injustice, which is against the divine nature, so that neither idols nor fortune can claim it.
Remarks that the apostolic account of heathen gods as demonic does not appear here beside the account of them as simply nothing.
